item.title: Stop Trying to Be Liked at Work
item.description:
Leadership

Stop Trying to Be Liked at Work

Why chasing approval can quietly undermine your credibility.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Seeking approval can weaken a leader's credibility when difficult decisions need to be made.
  • Being likeable is not the same as being liked. And the distinction matters.
  • Trust and respect are built through fairness, consistency and honest conversations, not popularity.
  • Strong working relationships don't require friendship, but they do require humanity.
Source: Andy Lopata / AI-Generated image

Most of us want our colleagues to like us. After all, we spend more of our time in the company of the people with whom we work than with anybody else, including family.

The relationships we build at work can shape our day-to-day experience and are a major factor in how happy we are in our jobs. A 2024 Catalyst survey found that the higher the quality of working relationships, the more likely employees were to report high job satisfaction and engagement. Retention increases and burnout levels drop.

We want to feel accepted and included, creating a strong pull to be part of the crowd and to be positively received. This desire for connection and acceptance is normal and, in many ways, positive.

For leaders, however, this instinct can undermine the very credibility they need to lead effectively.

The Problem With Trying to Be Liked

I started my first managerial role in my early twenties. Two of my team members were only a few years younger than me, in their late teens. I felt I had more in common with them than with my much older peers. Naturally, I acted more like their friend than their manager.

Although they reported to me, they also worked closely with other managers, who weren’t impressed with their performance and made their views very clear to me.

My friendships became an issue. I found myself softening colleagues’ criticisms because I didn’t want to come down too hard on people with whom I had become friends. But even the softer criticisms I shared landed badly with people who trusted me, seeming like a betrayal.

In the end, I disappointed both groups and learned a valuable lesson.

Perhaps it’s more natural for young people at the beginning of their careers to lean towards making friends at work, but the desire to be liked can be a challenge at all levels. When we want to be liked, we tend to over-accommodate and avoid difficult conversations. People-pleasers do not necessarily make great leaders; you need to challenge and provoke people to bring out the best in them and help them discover their own potential.

The Difference Between Being Liked and Being Likeable

Rather than seeking to be liked, leaders should focus on being likeable, according to Jenni Field, author of Nobody Believes You. Being likeable is less about popularity and more about how we show up with others — being approachable, respectful, easy to work with, and able to fit within a group without needing to be at its centre.

Field explained, “If I need to be liked, I’m focusing too much on the human need to belong and feel part of something.” She argues that being likeable is a more sustainable goal, especially at work, because it allows us to build good relationships without conflating them with friendship or universal approval.

“I think leaders and managers can get stuck wanting to be liked and not wanting to upset anyone. That becomes such a governing practice that it affects your ability to make difficult decisions and hard calls.”

When leaders try too hard to be liked, it can adversely affect their credibility within an organisation, precisely for these reasons. When we need to make tough choices, likeability can ensure they are more readily accepted.

Field sees likeability as part of credibility, rather than separate from it. As she explains, “If you are not likeable, if I don’t even want to be around you, then I’m not going to follow or believe in you.” Being likeable makes people more likely to listen to our arguments and take them seriously, rather than automatically challenging them.

Credibility relies on the respect we gain for making the right choices, not always the popular ones. People rarely follow leaders because they're popular; they follow those they trust to make good decisions.

Becoming a More Likeable Leader

Field suggests some simple, practical steps leaders can take to help them increase their likeability and, in turn, their credibility.

Seek Working Relationships, Not Friendships

At work, you don’t need to be everybody’s friend. But you do want people to feel that you are “nice to be around”. Make sure you have clear boundaries so that people understand that being friendly does not mean you are their personal friend.

Be Self-Aware

Understand how you come across to others and the impact your engagement style has on them. This might mean adjusting the pace at which you speak, your tone of voice, your tendency to overwhelm, or simply checking that instructions have been taken on board. It also means being willing to adapt if your message isn’t resonating.

Invest in Small Moments

Don’t try too hard to find rapport or build warmth. A cup of tea with a team member, whether through small talk or a simple check-in away from the transactional question of whether someone is doing their job effectively, can all help create connection.

Build Trust Before Challenging

If you are fair in most of your interactions with team members, you earn the right to challenge them constructively later. Don’t make every interaction a pushback; give praise and support first.

Bring in Other Perspectives to Reduce Bias

Having 360-degree reviews and perspectives from other leaders and colleagues can mitigate any perceived personal element in disagreements or challenges.

For leaders who are not naturally comfortable around others, this can be reassuring. Field’s message is not that everyone must become outwardly warm or socially fluent; rather, it is that likeability can be expressed in different ways. Being “nice to be around” might mean a calm presence, a quick cup of tea, a smile, or a small effort to connect, rather than forced sociability.

You don’t need everyone at work to like you. You just need to be someone they can work alongside comfortably and trust to do the right thing.

Leadership isn't about being everyone's friend. It's about becoming someone people trust, respect, and want to follow. Even when they don't always agree with you.

item.title: If You Cannot Beat Obesity, at Least Lower Its Complications
item.description:
Aging

If You Cannot Beat Obesity, at Least Lower Its Complications

Even without weight loss, you can slow down the damage of obesity.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Most complications related to obesity may be due to accelerated aging.
  • Weight loss is the best way to prevent obesity and age-related health issues.
  • However, without weight loss, we can also delay obesity-related aging complications.

Obesity is not just about the number on the scale. It quietly messes with your daily life. You buy clothes, and they do not fit right. Socially, people treat you differently, even if they do not say it. You start avoiding gatherings because you do not want to be judged. Over time, your confidence fades. You feel less capable, less visible. But here is the real kicker: While society judges your appearance, your body is paying a much heavier price. Diabetes, heart disease, memory problems, even cancer — they all become more likely. So, it is not just about looking good. It is about staying alive and feeling like yourself again.

What ultimately causes obesity to kill us is comorbidity with other illnesses. Most of these health consequences are common to diseases that accompany us as we age, yet they occur before obese people reach old age. In other words, obesity accelerates the rate of aging and the onset of age-related diseases.

Why does obesity speed aging?

Obesity promotes aging across multiple tissues and organs [1]. Based on new findings, aging begins with changes in the form and function of cells. This cellular aging, called senescence, was first described by Hayflick and Moorhead in the 1960s. They found that normal cells have a finite lifespan. After this time, they do not die but lose their ability to function and divide. Additionally, they release certain harmful chemical compounds, most of which are inflammatory molecules. These chemicals act as an "eat me" signal, attracting immune cells to eliminate them.

However, if these aged cells accumulate for any reason, these compounds can transfer their aged characteristics to neighboring healthy cells. Due to this ability, these cells are called "zombie cells." Zombie cells can also transmit aging to immune cells. There is a Persian proverb that says, "To prevent everything from spoiling, salt can be added, but woe to the day when the salt itself spoils." When the immune system ages, either due to chronological aging or through the transfer of aged cells, it is unable to remove these aged cells.

When we gain excessive weight due to overeating, the division of fat cells cannot keep up with the amount of synthesized fat that needs to be stored. So, they have to swell to create new capacity for storage of new fats. Swollen cells get stressed, and due to disruption of normal cell components and functions, they produce oxidative molecules that finally change them into aged cells. Immune cells are attracted to fat depots to eliminate these new zombie cells, but persistent overeating and excessive fat production overwhelm the immune system's battle, and ultimately the zombie cells win. This defeated army cannot remove zombie cells in other tissues, and the accumulation of aged cells accelerates the aging process throughout the body. Most struggles resulting from obesity come from complications associated with premature aging. Obesity speeds up nervous system, cardiovascular, pancreas, kidney, and immune system aging. Prolonged obesity even makes your appearance look more aged due to skin aging [2].

What should we do if we are obese?

The most reasonable approach is straightforward: weight loss through proper diets and more physical activity, but always under a nutritionist's supervision. This is the smartest way to reduce the aging effects and other complications that come with obesity. The key is to take it slow and turn it into a lifestyle, not a temporary fix. But here's the problem: People are always in a hurry. They want to lose weight before a party or a wedding. So, they go on crash diets, drop the pounds, and then gain everything back right after the event. That rebound weight gain is the real nightmare.

Lately, GLP-1 agonist drugs are being heavily advertised for weight loss. Personally, I avoid these new medications. They might have unknown side effects in the long run. Bariatric surgery is also an option for severe cases, but only under a specialist's care. However, even with surgery or medication, the risk of regaining weight is always there. None of these are magic solutions. At the end of the day, it all comes back to consistency, patience, and changing how we live, not just what we eat for a month.

If you cannot lose weight, at least follow these tips to prevent obesity-related aging

If you are struggling with weight loss and have been unable to reach your ideal weight, falling into a cycle of weight loss and regain, the very least you can do is avoid behaviors that worsen obesity-related aging and comorbidities.

1. Exercise regularly. Include both cardio and resistance training. Regular exercise reduces obesity and aging-related complications, slows cellular senescence, and boosts your immune system. Do not feel embarrassed about your body at the gym. You can be overweight but still have fewer complications. And do not get too hung up on weight loss through exercise — working out is beneficial even without losing a single pound [3].

2. Avoid processed foods and fast food. These are packed with empty calories, harmful oils, and chemical additives that trigger inflammation. They speed up aging and make obesity-related diseases worse.

3. Take care of your gut microbiome. Eat plenty of vegetables and prebiotic-rich foods like almonds, bananas, whole grain wheat, corn, rye, and barley. These help good bacteria thrive, improve diet outcomes, and protect against obesity-related complications [4].

4. Reduce stress and anxiety. Modern life is full of chronic stress. Social media makes us feel like we're always falling behind, always missing out. We constantly want to matter. And obesity itself is a constant source of stress — what they call "food noise," that endless worry about calories and weight. Studies show stress speeds up cellular aging and pushes obesity toward dangerous complications. Managing stress and getting regular sleep can slow down these harmful processes at the cellular level [5].

Overall, obesity speeds up aging at the cellular and systemic level, and most of its complications come from this process. Losing weight and following some basic tips can help us manage these issues better.

item.title: Long-Term Side Effects of Antipsychotics
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Long-Term Side Effects of Antipsychotics

Why long-term monitoring matters as much as the initial prescription.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Long-term antipsychotic use may lead to metabolic, hormonal, and movement disorders.
  • Tardive dyskinesia and other movement disorders can be difficult to treat and, in some cases, irreversible.
  • Despite these risks, antipsychotic treatment is linked to lower overall mortality.
Source: Tiago Bandeira / Unsplash

When people talk about side effects, they usually mean the ones that show up shortly after starting a medication, such as dizziness, drowsiness, or tremors. The long-term effects, which may emerge only after years of treatment, are often overlooked or not discussed.

When it comes to antipsychotics, these effects are well documented in the literature and include dyslipidemia, movement disorders, hormonal imbalances, and neurological changes.

These are important issues that, over the course of treatment, often go undiscussed, either because they take so long to develop or out of concern about frightening the patient and reducing treatment adherence. But they shouldn't just be discussed. They should also be monitored during follow-up visits, whether through laboratory tests (in the case of dyslipidemia and hormonal dysfunction) or clinical assessments.

This conversation matters both for supporting patient autonomy whenever possible and for helping families understand potential risks and prevent future complications.

Types of Antipsychotics

Not all antipsychotics are alike. Older, first-generation or "typical" antipsychotics tend to cause more intense side effects. Second-generation drugs, known as "atypical," have a different profile of risks and benefits and are generally better tolerated by many patients.

Second-generation medications have been prescribed with increasing frequency, now accounting for more than 90% of antipsychotic use in many countries around the world. The main barrier to their use is cost.

Long-Term Effects

Beyond the more immediate effects, like drowsiness, tremors, and increased appetite, antipsychotics can cause effects that only appear years after treatment begins.

Metabolic effects, specifically metabolic syndrome, are characterized by:

  • Weight gain
  • Elevated blood sugar levels
  • Elevated cholesterol

Together, these raise cardiovascular risk.

Hormonal effects include:

  • Elevated prolactin levels, which can lead to gynecomastia in men
  • Sexual dysfunction and reduced libido, caused by disruption of testosterone and estrogen levels
  • Menstrual irregularities, also linked to changes in estrogen levels
article continues after advertisement

Movement disorders, typically present in both acute and chronic (tardive) forms. The acute presentation, which typically appears early in treatment, is relatively common and treatable. But these disorders can also emerge after years of treatment, often progressively and in ways that are difficult to manage.

  • Tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder marked by involuntary movements that usually involve the tongue, face, mouth, and jaw. In some cases, the condition is irreversible even after the medication is discontinued.
  • Chronic akathisia, a state of restlessness and an intense need to keep moving. The acute version is more common and tends to improve over time or with changes in pharmacotherapy, while the chronic version can be harder to treat.
  • Tardive dystonia, characterized by twisting, repetitive postures resulting from transient or intermittent spasms of antagonistic muscle groups.

Mortality: What Effect Do Antipsychotics Have?

People with schizophrenia have a life expectancy that is, on average, 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population. This mortality gap has been observed across diverse populations.

However, when comparing treated and untreated groups of patients, overall mortality is higher among untreated patients than among those who receive antipsychotic treatment.

article continues after advertisement

Cardiovascular disorders, especially acute myocardial infarction and coronary artery disease, are leading causes of sudden death in schizophrenia. This may be explained in part by the metabolic effects of antipsychotic medications.

In addition, suicide rates are higher among people with schizophrenia than in the general population, including those receiving treatment.

Addressing Side Effects Without Causing Alarm

Given the existence of both chronic, late-emerging effects and acute ones, how we talk to patients and families about these possibilities matters even more. The line between informing and frightening is a thin one.

Still, it is essential that patients understand the potential effects so they can recognize early warning signs. When this isn't possible, the family should be informed instead.

One thing worth keeping in mind is that when someone experiences an unpleasant effect without understanding what it is, they may abandon treatment altogether, something that's common with psychotropic medications.

How can this be communicated without frightening the patient? Ideally, by using terms the patient and family can understand, emphasizing the importance of treatment, and keeping an open line of communication with the care team so that management can be as effective as possible.

It is also important not to overwhelm the conversation with risks all at once. Treatment is a long process, with periodic visits, so information can be shared gradually as treatment progresses.

item.title: A Neuroscience Perspective on the Concept of Self in IFS
item.description:
Neuroscience

A Neuroscience Perspective on the Concept of Self in IFS

A balanced brain supports a curious, compassionate mind.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • IFS aims to develop secure inner attachments between a resource called Self and parts, or subpersonalities.
  • Self displays curiosity, calm, clarity, connectedness, confidence, courage, creativity, and compassion.
  • Neuroscience tells us that a balanced brain supports those same qualities.

Co-authored with Sarah Bergenfield

Do you ever suddenly become calmer, more curious, and more compassionate, not because your problems disappeared but because something shifted inside? From the perspective of Internal Family Systems (IFS), you're experiencing a distinct state of consciousness called Self. IFS is all about engaging this kind of consciousness in the context of the idea that the mind is plural: We all have parts (as in, one part of me wants to go for a walk, but another wants to take a nap).

If you wonder what parts are, we can’t tell you. We can only describe the experience. They are individuals, each with their own developmental age, experiences, and perspective. They live in a community and share the ultimate goals of survival and safety. Self, on the other hand, is not a part. It’s more like a compass for the inner community of parts. Most people grasp Self best experientially, but sometimes we need words to introduce and explain the concept. When this need arises, IFS practitioners tend to reach for metaphors that hail from physics and spiritual traditions. While these serve well for some people, they’re too abstract for others.

So, here's another option. Neuroscience tells us that the brain builds a predictive model of the world beginning in childhood and then experiences what it predicts, registering prediction errors throughout life to update its model. In the process, it must decide which errors deserve conscious attention (signal) and which do not (noise). Most prediction errors, as it turns out, are inconsequential and can safely receive an automatic, unconscious update (the mug on the counter has moved since I was in the kitchen this morning). But sometimes a mismatch is worth conscious notice (wait a minute – I thought I was alone in the house) and it leads to feeling uncertain.

Uncertainty can arise from experiences along a continuum from the simple inconvenience (I can’t find my keys. Why did I walk into this room? When will Joe text me?) to the very big deal (I got fired, my spouse is leaving me, I’ve been diagnosed with cancer, my father just died of a heart attack). While events along this continuum are likely to have widely varying impacts, they share one critical effect: They create uncertainty.

The brain prefers certainty. Since we expend less energy and function better when the world makes sense, the brain is always striving to predict with accuracy. At the same time, prediction errors propel learning. We need uncertainty, but just enough. Too much overwhelms; enough enlivens. The trick is to balance surprise and predictability. Take travel, for example. When we travel, we’re looking for rousing doses of surprise. If that’s what happens, we return feeling refreshed, and we see new angles to routine environments.

Contrast this with irresolvable uncertainty. Faced with unpredictability that cannot be reduced through learning or action, protective parts work to make things predictable again by constructing coherent explanations about other people, ourselves, and the world. These stories may or may not be accurate, but in the moment they reduce uncertainty and make experience feel more manageable. By the time the limitations of these invented stories become apparent, they are often deeply held, hard-to-shake predictions that color our beliefs and expectations in subtle or extreme ways. Every solution has benefits and costs.

Source: loaivat/Pixabay

IFS conducts internal inquiries, which usually start with curiosity about the protectors who are trying to ward off uncertainty and make the world more predictable by controlling other parts and other people. To approach them respectfully, without judgment, we need the brain to be flexible and capable of holding multiple perspectives without being defensive. IFS calls this state of mind Self. In the language of predictive processing, we propose that Self emerges when the brain reaches a state of balanced precision, a computational sweet spot in which neither prior expectations nor real-time sensory information are given excessive importance. In this state, the brain can hold expectations lightly, see prediction errors as opportunities for learning, and update its world model efficiently. Isn’t that what we want?

Here are the core qualities that show up in the brain on Self. IFS calls them the 8 Cs:

Curiosity: When we are curious, prediction errors function as useful information. In the language of IFS, they are a trailhead.

Clarity: The balanced brain discerns noteworthy signals from unimportant background noise.

Confidence: Confidence doesn't come from certainty. It comes from trusting that mistakes and failures will improve our model of the world.

Creativity: Creativity requires uncertainty. Flexible brains generate possibilities instead of defending certainty.

Connectedness: The balanced brain can take in multiple perspectives at once and appreciate the kernel of truth or importance in each.

Calm: A nervous system that is free of overly-precise threat predictions can engage alertly, like a skilled athlete.

Courage: Parts who are connected with Self have the courage to abide uncertainty and update even deeply held predictions.

Compassion: In a state of balance, we are able to be compassionate. We are curious about parts, feeling for them with a stance of caring, concern, and the willingness to act on their behalf. Self asks: What uncertainty is this part trying to resolve?

We’re not suggesting that predictive processing can fully explain the nature of Self or that neuroscience can replace the inquiry of IFS into subjective experience. Rather, it offers a plausible account of the computational conditions under which Self emerges. When the brain is in a state of balanced precision, neither clinging to existing beliefs nor overwhelmed by new information, it is flexible, open to learning, and ready for whatever comes. IFS calls this experience Self-energy. Understanding Self in this way bridges first-person experience and neuroscience, making a profound idea more accessible without diminishing its mystery. Some experiences remain difficult to capture in words. Self may be one of them. But if neuroscience helps more people recognize and trust this state within, let’s bring it to the conversation.

item.title: Why Trying to "Be Good" With Food Can Backfire
item.description:
Appetite

Why Trying to "Be Good" With Food Can Backfire

Losing control with food may be the result of attempting to follow rules.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Restrictive eating is a trap.
  • Research suggests the effort to restrict is linked to loss-of-control eating.
  • Labeling your eating as "good" or "bad" turns it into a moral test you can pass or fail.
  • Consistent, flexible eating creates a pathway to nourishing your body and healing your mind.
Source: Spencer Davis / Unsplash

This post was written by Gia Marson, EdD

Have you ever promised yourself you'd "be good" with food this week, only to find yourself eating in a way that felt out of control? If so, you are not weak, and you are not alone. That pattern isn't a personal failing. It's often the predictable result of the rules you adopted.

When food becomes a moral test

We tend to talk about food in the language of morality. Some foods are referred to as "clean," "safe," or "good"; others are "junk," "cheat," or "bad." Eating the first kind can make us feel virtuous; eating the second, guilty. A recent qualitative study of restrictive eating found that people often build a sense of moral identity around dietary discipline, experiencing strict eating as a demonstration of virtue and self-control. And when we apply moral messaging to conversations about eating, even a minor step away from what we're told is ideal can negatively affect our self-talk and how we see ourselves. In other words, following rigid dietary rules becomes conflated with being a good person.

Restriction, rebranded as wellness

This message is everywhere, and social media adds fuel to it. In 2025, researchers analyzed roughly 100,000 Instagram posts about food and eating and found that content representing restrictive diets and approaches to eating were pervasive. A 2024 study of online wellness images and content found that they normalize food restriction as natural and admirable, worsening how people feel about their bodies:

"…while in the past these tendencies were found among public figures or those associated with political, artistic, or beauty fields, today it is common and considerably more concerning, as personal value is increasingly associated with the ability to meet certain beauty standards, even at younger ages." — Zaharia & Gonța, 2024

Source: Photo by Yumu (愚木混株) on Unsplash

This may be surprising: The effort is the risk

When researchers followed adolescents in real time, tracking their eating throughout the day, they found something counterintuitive: It was the attempt to restrict, not whether the person actually ate less, that was associated with later loss-of-control eating. Trying to limit consumption was itself the risk. The mental effort of monitoring, resisting, and forbidding seemed to set up the very loss of control it was supposed to prevent.

Why would attempting to restrict make things worse? Because rigid, rule-bound eating works against your biology and your psychology at the same time. Trying not to eat enough sets off an internal alarm because your body wants enough food to meet your energy needs and activity level. Therefore, your body begins to urge you to eat more as a way to maintain or return to homeostasis. Furthermore, planning to eat less leads to a preoccupation with food that may interfere with your natural hunger and fullness cues and with your ability to concentrate in other parts of your life. The bottom line: trying to undereat is unnatural.

What helps? Fewer rules and less moral judgment

The goal is to make eating a little boring again, in the best possible sense: predictable, adequate, satisfying, and flexible. That means eating regularly enough that you're not running on empty, including foods you genuinely enjoy, and not using eating as evidence for or against your worth. When food stops being an all-or-nothing test of your goodness, it can simply be a way to nourish yourself.

If this pattern of restricting your eating and then losing control is familiar to you, recognizing and accepting it is a starting point for change. However, if your relationship with food feels distressing or hard to manage on your own, please consider reaching out to a qualified professional. Support helps.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What Is Black Matrescence?
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

What Is Black Matrescence?

The transition to Black motherhood finally has a name.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Black matrescence names the racialized psychological transition into motherhood.
  • Racism shapes the conditions of pregnancy and motherhood, not just the stress layered on top.
  • Black mothers often carry racial vigilance and deep joy through the same transition.
  • Structural support, not individual coping alone, determines how well mothers recover.

When a baby arrives, the world leans toward the child, asking whether she is sleeping, feeding, growing on schedule. Much less often does anyone ask what is happening inside the woman who just became a mother, even though her transformation is just as real and just as demanding of our attention.

Motherhood is not a role simply added onto an unchanged life. It can quietly reorganize how a woman understands her body, her relationships, her ambitions, and the core of who she believes herself to be. Psychologists call this developmental process matrescence, a term that mirrors adolescence in the way it describes a profound shift in identity. A woman may recognize her own face in the mirror while feeling, underneath, like someone entirely new.

What often goes unspoken is that matrescence does not move through every woman's life the same way. For Black women, the transition into motherhood, or Black matrescence, unfolds inside a deeply racialized social world, shaped by medical racism, reproductive vulnerability, cultural expectations of strength, and the weight of raising a Black child in a society that has never fully guaranteed that child's safety.

The mother is developing, too

So much of how we talk about motherhood centers on what a woman must do for the baby and for her family. Matrescence asks a different question, one that gets asked far too rarely: Who is she becoming underneath all of that doing? Her body may stop feeling entirely familiar. Her friendships shift. Her career may feel newly urgent or suddenly complicated to hold alongside everything else. She may quietly grieve the freedom and spontaneity that once defined her days.

These feelings are hard to speak aloud because our culture narrates motherhood almost exclusively through gratitude. However, the truth is often much messier, and many mothers fear that honesty will be mistaken for regret. A mother can feel fiercely attached to her child while still missing the person she used to be — grateful and overwhelmed, all in the same afternoon.

Matrescence does not exist outside of race

A Black woman may walk into pregnancy already carrying the awareness that her pain could be dismissed, her concerns minimized, her knowledge of her own body questioned by the very people meant to care for her. She may monitor how forcefully she advocates for herself, worried that naming her fear will make her seem unstable while naming her anger will make her seem difficult. The transition can ask her to become patient and advocate, mother and protector, all while trusting systems that have not always earned it.

Motherhood can change the way race feels

A woman becoming a mother is no longer only thinking about how racism touches her own body and safety. She begins imagining how the world will perceive her child, when he will first be stereotyped or disciplined more harshly than his peers. This is one of the defining features of Black matrescence: a mother is not only adapting to caring for a child, but she is also learning to mother inside a society where protection can never be fully promised. That reality can deepen love and cultural connection. It can also produce vigilance, fear, and grief that deserve to be honored rather than hidden.

Joy and community are part of this story too

None of this means Black matrescence is only weight and worry. Alongside the vigilance runs something equally real: a deep well of joy, connection, and cultural inheritance that shapes this transition just as powerfully as racism does.

Black mothers often step into motherhood surrounded by a wide circle of care that many other cultures have lost touch with. Grandmothers, aunties, church mothers, sister-friends, and neighbors show up with meals, wisdom, and hands ready to hold a baby so a new mother can sleep. Mothering, in many Black communities, has never been meant to happen alone, and that collective care can soften even the hardest parts of the transition.

There is also a particular joy in watching a child grow into their own Black identity; in braiding hair with a technique passed down through generations, in choosing a name that carries ancestry, in teaching a toddler to clap along to music that has been sung in the family for decades. These moments carry pride, continuity, and a sense of belonging that can anchor a mother even as she navigates fear for her child's safety.

Black matrescence holds both of these truths without asking one to cancel out the other. A mother can feel the weight of raising a Black child in an unsafe world and also feel profound delight in who that child is becoming, surrounded by people who love them fiercely. The joy is not a distraction from the hard parts. It is part of what makes the transition survivable, and part of what makes it beautiful.

The expectation to be strong

Black women are so often praised for resilience, and strength runs through Black cultural identity as a thread of survival, faith, and collective care. But strength can harden into an expectation that leaves little room for softness when a woman needs it most. A Black mother may be praised for how well she seems to be handling everything while she is privately unraveling behind closed doors. Family, workplaces, and even close friends may offer her less support because she looks like she doesn't need it. That pressure can make it painfully hard to say the truest things: that she is scared, that she needs help, that she loves her baby and is struggling all at once. Black matrescence has to leave room for those words.

Not every difficult emotion is a disorder

The emotional shifts of matrescence can look like symptoms of distress, and naming this transition can help a woman stop interpreting every hard feeling as personal failure. At the same time, this concept should never wave away symptoms that are genuinely serious. Postpartum depression, anxiety, and psychosis all require careful care, and Black women already face real barriers to receiving it. We need to hold two truths at once: not every painful part of becoming a mother is a disorder, and not every severe symptom is simply a normal adjustment.

Black matrescence is personal and structural

Mothers are told to rest, set boundaries, and practice mindfulness. These strategies can offer comfort, but they cannot correct the structural conditions surrounding motherhood. A mother cannot meditate her way into paid leave, or breathe deeply enough to dissolve medical racism or housing instability. Her distress cannot always be understood as something happening only inside her own mind. Sometimes her anxiety is a reasonable response to a genuinely unsafe system.

Why naming Black matrescence matters

Language shapes what we allow ourselves to notice. Naming Black matrescence lets clinicians ask not only whether a mother is depressed, but how motherhood has reshaped her identity, her racial awareness, and her sense of safety. It asks families and communities to support the mother as a person who is still becoming, not only as the one everyone else depends on. Black matrescence also gives a name to the deeply racialized and nuanced process of becoming a mother.

item.title: The Power of Walking Around the Block
item.description:
Trauma

The Power of Walking Around the Block

The first steps post-trauma are literal steps.

Posted July 20, 2026

This post is part 1 of a series.

This week, like most weeks this year, disasters have happened around the world that have irrevocably changed people’s lives: Earthquakes in Peru and Venezuela, Flooding in Laos, Wildfires in Canada and the US and many many more events that barely made the news.

In April, my suburb in Wellington, New Zealand was hit by the heaviest rainfall for the area on record. The amount of rain that normally falls in half a month in April, came crashing down in one hour. At 3.30am, we were woken by the intense noise of rain on the roof and pipes gurgling. A few minutes later we saw some rain coming through the gap under our front door, but by the time we ran to get towels we realized it was too late. The water could not be stopped. We woke the children and told them to sit on the couch, but soon the couch was floating. By 4am, we were waist-deep in water throughout the house. We climbed into our attic and waited for the fire department to come and help us evacuate across the river that was flowing where our street had been. We spent the next week throwing out everything in our house that was below waist height, including the carpet and insulation behind the walls, along with all our furniture, whiteware, shoes, toys and books. The worst part was telling our children that our cat had drowned under the house. In the past few months we have had to find a home to rent, borrow furniture and deal with insurance and tradespeople. All of this while we still have our regular busy lives, jobs, school, activities.

I’m a psychologist who works with trauma, stress and life changes. One of the many things that has been frequently running through my brain (in between worrying about whether my kids are ok and then trying to remember details for insurance claims or make rebuilding decisions) is to ask myself whether I can say that I’ve been genuinely following the advice I would give to clients I work with. Every day I talk to people who have been through awful life experiences and they look at me like I’m the expert with all the right advice. More specifically, I’ve been reflecting on whether the principles of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which are the ideas I have based my books Holding the Heavy Stuff and Stuff that Sucks on, help me in trauma.

Spoiler alert: Yes, they have. But also, it wasn’t easy. Knowing what helps doesn’t always make it easy to do.

Five days after the flood, the day after we had finished loading up a sixth giant dumpster bin with our belongings, I lay in bed. Well, I say ‘bed’, but it was a sofa bed in the home of our very kind friends who had us stay for that first week. I was done. I felt I had to avoid my kids because I was supposed to be putting on a brave face for them and I just wanted to sob (but annoyingly my body wouldn’t even let me do that yet). I couldn’t imagine how we could begin to rebuild and live with the anxiety of waiting for another one-in-a-hundred year storm (they seem to happen every few weeks these days).

My wife suggested that we go for a short walk. I didn’t want to leave the bed. I just wanted to lie there, feeling sorry for myself, ruminating over how hard everything was. But I also knew that taking a walk around the block would be the exact advice I would give to a client who had been through similar challenges. I reluctantly got out of bed and threw some clothes on and we went for a 15-minute walk.

It really was only 15 minutes but it was all I needed to catch my breath and to take a break from my doom-spiraling brain. It was all I needed to notice that in this moment, we have a place to stay, we all got out, and we were going to figure it out one step at a time.

So why does a brief walk help? It didn’t fix my house, nor give me any solutions. But it woke my senses up – seeing, hearing, feeling where I am right now. Right now is the only time we can do anything, whereas when we are down, our minds want to problem-solve things that have already happened or how to deal with possible futures. Feeling the sun on my face also helped my body notice that the rain had stopped and the storm had passed. Walking with my wife allowed us to connect to what really matters: how we best support our kids and ourselves today. Bumping into a friend on the walk allowed me to receive a much-needed hug and some caring.

In my next few posts, I will talk about how I used each of the ACT processes to help me manage losing our house and our cat — and having to rethink everything I thought I knew about where our life was heading. But please remember, the starting point after a trauma is the small things – hugs, walks around the block, feeling the sunshine, catching your breath. Without these small steps, there’s no opportunity for the bigger steps that come next.
